'''asomatous''' (a-sō′ma-tus), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀσώματος, without a body, < ἀ- priv. + σῶμα(τ-), body.] Without a material body; incorporeal. [Rare.]

'''Asopia''' (a-sō′pi-ä), ''n.'' [NL.; cf. ''Asopus''.] A genus of pyralid moths. ''A. farinalis'' is the meal-moth.

'''Asopinæ''' (as-ō-pī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asopus'' + ''-inæ''.] A subfamily of heteropterous insects, typified by the genus ''Asopus''. Also ''Asopina''.

'''Asopus''' (a-sō′pus), ''n.'' [NL., appar. < L. ''Asōpus'', Gr. Ἀσωπός, name of several rivers and of a river-god.] A genus of heteropterous insects, of the family ''Pentatomidæ''.

'''asor''' (as′ôr), ''n.'' [Heb.] A ten-stringed musical instrument of the Hebrews, played with a plectrum, and supposed to have borne some resemblance to the nebel. ''S. K. Handbook Mus. Inst.'', p. 19.

'''asp<sup>1</sup>''' (asp), ''n.'' [< ME. ''asp'', ''aspe'', ''espe'', < AS. *''æsp'', ''æspe'', ''aspe'', ''espe'', transposed ''æps'', = D. ''esp'' = OHG. ''aspa'', MHG. ''aspe'', G. ''espe'' = Icel. ''ösp'', asp, ''espi'', aspen wood, = Dan. Sw. ''asp'', asp; origin unknown. The E. form ''aspen'' is prop. an adj.: see ''aspen''.] A European tree of the poplar family, ''Populus tremula''. {{smaller|In America a similar species, ''P. tremuloides'', is known as the quaking asp, or aspen. The white poplar, ''P. alba'', is also sometimes called the ''white asp''. The form ''aspen'' is also common.}}

''aspis'' (''aspid-''), < Gr. ἀσπίς (ἀσπιδ-), an asp, Egyptian viper.]   '''1.''' '''asparagus''' (as-par′a-gus), ''n.''   [< L. ''asparagus'', < Gr. ἀσπάραγος, Attic ἀσφάραγος, asparagus; said to be of Pers. origin. In ML. by apheresis also ''sparagus, sparagi'', > It. ''sparagio'', OF. ''esperage'', > early mod. E. ''sperage, sparage, sperach.'' The ML. form ''sparagus'' was in E. altered by popular etymology into ''sparagrass'' and ''sparrow-grass'' (sometimes simply ''grass''), which were until recently in good literary use.]   '''1.''' A plant of the genus ''Asparagus'', especially ''A. officinalis.''—'''2.''' [''cap.''] A large genus of plants of the old world, natural order ''Liliaceæ.'' {{smaller|That which is cultivated in gardens, the common asparagus, or ''Asparagus officinalis'', has a much-branched stem rising from thick and matted perennial root-stocks, and small greenish-yellow flowers. The narrow thread-like so-called leaves are in reality branchlets growing in clusters in the axils of the true but scale-like leaves. The roots have a bitterish mucilaginous taste, and the stalk is in some degree aperient and deobstruent, but not very efficacious. The part eaten is the turion, or young shoot covered with scales in place of leaves. The sprouts contain the crystalline substance called ''asparagin.''—'''French''' or '''Prussian asparagus''', a name in some parts of England for the fleshy spike of ''Ornithogalum Pyrenaicum.''}} '''asparagus-bean''' (as-par′ạ-gus-bēn), ''n.'' See ''bean''1, 1. '''asparagus-beetle''' (as-par′ạ-gus-bē″tl), ''n.'' A name given to two species of leaf-beetles (''Crioceridæ'') of the genus ''Crioceris'', ''C. asparagi'' (Linnæus) and ''C. duodecimpunctata'' (Linnæus), which prey upon the asparagus-plant. {{smaller block| {{img float|file=century v01 p0365 c2f1.png|width=242px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Asparagus-beetle (''Crioceris asparagi'').}}
{{smaller|''a'', ''b'', ''d'', and ''e'', beetle, eggs, and larvæ, natural size; ''c'' and ''f'', eggs and larva, enlarged.}}}} Both species were imported into the United States from Europe. Both the beetles and their larvæ feed upon the asparagus-plant, but the damage is principally done by the larvæ. ''C. asparagi'' is blackish beneath, the thorax being reddish above, and the elytra ornamented with yellowish spots of varying extent. ''C. duodecimpunctata'' is nearly uniformly reddish, the elytra having twelve small black spots. The larvæ of the two species resemble each other closely; they are nearly cylindrical, tapering somewhat toward the head, shining, and of a dirty olive-green color.}} '''asparagus-stone''' (as-par′ạ-gus-stōn), ''n.'' A yellowish-green variety of the mineral apatite, occurring in Spain in small transparent crystals. '''asparamide''' (as-par′a̤-mid), ''n.''   [< ''aspar(agin)'' + ''amide.'']   Same as ''asparagin.'' '''asparginic''' (as-pär-jin′ik), ''a.''   [< ''aspar(a)gin'' + ''-ic.'']   Same as ''aspartic.'' '''asparmate''' (as-pär′māt), ''n.''   [< ''aspar(a)m(ide)'' + ''-ate''1.]   Same as ''aspartate.'' '''aspartate''' (as-pär′tāt), ''n.''   [< ''aspart(ic)'' + ''-ate''1.]   Any salt of aspartic acid. Also ''asparagic, asparginic.''—{{smaller|'''Aspartic acid,''' C4H7NO4, a crystalline acid derived from asparagin.}} '''aspe†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''asp''1 and ''asp''2. '''aspect''' (as′pekt, formerly as-pekt′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''aspect'', < L. ''aspectus'', seeing, look, appearance, countenance, < ''aspicere'', look, behold, < ''ad'', to, + ''specere'', look: see ''species'' and ''spy.'']   '''1.''' The act of seeing, or of looking at anything; view; gaze; glance; look. [Archaic.] {{smaller block|Some other mistress hath thy sweet ''aspects.'' {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|His ''aspect'' was bent on the ground. {{right|''Scott.''}}}} {{smaller block|Meeting the cold ''aspect'' of Duty. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Autocrat, xi.}}}} '''2.''' Countenance; look or particular appearance of the face; mien; air: as, a mild or severe ''aspect.'' {{smaller block|Wiser princes patron the arts, and carry an indulgent ''aspect'' unto scholars. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Yet, had his ''aspect'' nothing of severe, But such a face as promis’d him sincere. {{right|''Dryden'', Character of Good Parson, i. 12.}}}} '''3.''' Appearance to the eye or mind; look: as, the physical ''aspect'' of the country. {{smaller block|And then our arms, like to a muzzled bear, Save in ''aspect'', have all offence seal’d up. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|How sweet, how fair, and lovely her ''aspects'' are! Her eyes, like bright Eoan flames, shoot through me. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Prophetess, iii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|What a collegiate ''aspect'' has that fine Elizabethan hall, where the fountain plays! {{right|''Lamb'', Old Benchers.}}}} '''4.''' One of the ways in which a thing may be viewed or contemplated: as, to present an object or a subject in its true ''aspect''; in a double ''aspect''; a favorable ''aspect''. {{smaller block|Something loftier, more adorned, Than is the common ''aspect'', daily garb, Of human life. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, v.}} Undoubtedly we have a right to make new words, as they are needed by the fresh ''aspects'' under which life presents itself here in the New World; and, indeed, wherever a language is alive, it grows. {{right|''Lowell'', Introd. to Biglow Papers, 1st ser.}}}} '''5.''' Practical bearing or reference. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The ''aspect'' of atonement is obviously toward creatures, working effects on them, not on God. {{right|''J. Gilbert'', Christ. Atonement, p. 167. (''N. E. D.'')}}}} '''6.''' View commanded; prospect; outlook. {{smaller block|This town has a good ''aspect'' toward the hill from whence we descended. {{right|''Evelyn.''}}}} {{smaller block|[Now used in this sense mainly with reference to the points of the compass: as, a house has a southern ''aspect'' or exposure.]}} '''7.''' In ''astrol.'', the relative positions of the planets as they appear at any given time to an observer upon the earth; the combined look of the heavenly bodies from the earth. {{smaller|The aspects are nine in number: (1) semisextile, a difference of longitude of 30°; (2) semisquare, of 45°; (3) sextile, of 60°; (4) quintile, of 72°; (5) square or quartile, of 90°; (6) trine, of 120°; (7) sesquiquadrate, of 135°; (8) biquintile, of 144°; (9) opposition, of 180°. To these may be added conjunction, which occurs when the planets have the same longitude. ''Good aspects'' are the semisextile, sextile, quintile, trine, and biquintile. ''Bad aspects'' are the semisquare, square, sesquiquadrate, and opposition. ''Mundane aspects'' are such as are formed by the houses in horary astrology and by the semiarcs of the planets in nativities.}} {{smaller block|The glorious planet, Sol, . . . whose med′cinable eye Corrects the ill ''aspects'' of planets evil. {{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|We, that behold the sad ''aspects'' of heaven, Leading sense-blinded men, feel grief enough To know, though not to speak, their miseries. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iii. 3.}}}} '''8.''' In ''her.'', the position of an animal with reference to the spectator.—{{smaller|'''Ambulacral aspect.''' See ''ambulacral.''—'''Aspect of a plane,''' in ''math.'', the direction of its normal.—'''In full aspect.''' Same as ''affronté'', 2.—'''In trian aspect,''' in a position between ''affronté'' and ''passant.''—'''Mesial aspect.''' See ''mesial.''}} '''aspect†''' (as-pekt′), ''v. t.''   [< L. Capable of being seen; visible. {{smaller block|What is in this ''aspectable'' world? {{right|''Ray'', Creation.}}}} '''2.''' Fair or fit to be seen. {{smaller block|Via Vittoria, the ''aspectable'' street Where he lived mainly. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 57.}}}} [Rare in both senses.] '''aspectant''' (as-pek′tant), ''a.''   [< L.
